newsitem.title: USA: Clinton undergoes surgery to repair knee injury.
newsitem.headline: Clinton undergoes surgery to repair knee injury.

text.p: President Bill Clinton underwent surgery on Friday to repair a torn knee tendon. Aides said he was in good spirits, determined to keep a summit date with Boris Yeltsin and dreaming of golfing and jogging again.

The knee-buckling tumble on the Florida estate of golfer Greg Norman -- "he heard a very loud pop," one aide said -- will put Clinton on crutches for weeks, but he insisted it would not delay his summit with the Russian president in Helsinki, Finland, next week.

"The president informed the doctors that he will be going to Helsinki on Tuesday and they said, 'yes sir,' they understood that," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said as surgery began at Bethesda Naval Hospital near Washington.
On his departure from West Palm Beach, Fla., Clinton insisted he would proceed, saying, "It will go on, you bet."

First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, at her husband's side at the hospital, planned to go ahead with a two-week tour of six African nations, but was likely to delay her departure on Saturday by a few hours at least.

McCurry said the incident was also one factor in the postponement of the planned White House visit of Jordan's King Hussein scheduled for Tuesday. Hussein's visit had been in doubt anyway due to the faltering pace of the Middle East peace process.
Doctors performed an epidural or "regional" anaesthetic that numbs the body from the mid-section down at 1:50 p.m. EST (1850 GMT) and Clinton reacted fine, McCurry said.
A regional anaesthetic allows Clinton to remain conscious during the surgery, avoiding a temporary transfer of presidential powers to Vice President Al Gore, who was travelling in California.
McCurry said doctors began surgery at 2:39 p.m. EST (1939 GMT).
Doctors had to drill holes in the kneecap and in the tendon and run sutures through the holes to reattach the tendon, which controls the ability to straighten the leg.
"This is not a terribly severe injury and not a terribly complicated operation to perform," said Dr. David Wade, chief of the naval hospital's clinical staff.
Instead of a cast, his knee will be placed in a brace to give him some mobility but to protect the leg, Wade said.
McCurry said Clinton asked typical patient's questions such as how long it would be before he could run or swing a golf club again.

Wade said Clinton would remain at least overnight at the hospital and possibly until Sunday, then faced four to five months of rehabilitation before he can hit golf balls again, and perhaps six months before he can jog.

Said McCurry: "He's feeling very good about it (the operation) and is anxious to get it done ... He's in a little bit of pain when the leg moves but he's in very good spirits. He's joking around with a lot of us. He keeps saying he's got work to do."

Looking ahead to a planned weekend of golf, Clinton stumbled on a step at the Florida estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman early on Friday, tearing the quadriceps tendon connecting the kneecap to the upper thigh in his right leg.

He made a dramatic arrival at Andrews Air Force Base after his Air Force One flight from Florida. A blue elevator truck raised a platform from the rain-slick tarmac to the front door of the plane. Secret Service agents helped him on board and he was lowered to the ground.

He emerged with a crutch under his right arm and his left arm around the shoulders of a Secret Service agent. Someone held a large black umbrella over his head as he hopped left-footed to a black recreation vehicle in a driving rain. Mrs. Clinton hovered nearby, overseeing his progress.

A senior State Department official said another possible diplomatic casualty of the presidential mishap could be a scheduled Monday meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, which might have to be scrapped. Primakov arrives in Washington over the weekend for talks to prepare the Helsinki summit.
